newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: FEATURE - No fireworks to mark Slovenia's sixth birthday.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - No fireworks to mark Slovenia's sixth birthday.

text.p: Six years after Slovenia's dramatic breakaway from former Yugoslavia, euphoria has faded and a new sense of political and economic realism pervades the capital's neat streets.
Ljubljana's declaration of independence on June 26, 1991 precipitated a 10-day bloody conflict that involved the first air strike in Europe since the end of World War Two.

Yet only 1,500 mainly public figures are expected to attend a June 25 gathering in the capital's cultural centre to mark the anniversary this year -- a far cry from the throngs that braved torrential rain to dance through the city last summer.

That party, which began with a military parade and ended at midnight with a spectacular firework display, came just days after Slovenia signed a long-awaited association agreement with the European Union.

Today the dawning realisation that genuine integration into the West is a tortuous process has put a damper on the event -- a mix of music and ballet to be opened with a speech by President Milan Kucan.
About as large as Canada's Lake Ontario, with Alpine peaks and a Mediterranean coast, Slovenia is the richest of Europe's former communist countries with per capita GDP of $9,362.
But unemployment at over 14 percent is stubbornly high compared with five percent pre-independence. Other economic and political storm clouds are also beginning to gather.

U.S. support for Slovenia's speedy inclusion in the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) has evaporated, knocking the nation's fragile confidence and its hopes of an early entry into the European Union.
"For our long term interests we believe it would be better for Slovenia to be included in NATO," Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek said.

"Missing out on NATO would be a bad blow to Slovenia as it would slow down its integration into the developed world and thus may put a brake on its further development," a political analyst explained.
He said missing out on NATO would undermine Slovenia's EU ambitions -- already in doubt because of its reluctance to ratify last year's association accord.
The courts have ruled that parliament must amend the constitution before ratification to allow foreigners to buy real estate, bringing Slovenian law into line with EU norms .

But parliamentary parties have yet to agree on the timing of a vote and, although Prime Minister Drnovsek has said he expects the necessary changes in July, some analysts believe it may take months to reach an agreement.

"If ratification does not go ahead this year, Slovenia will be in serious danger of missing the first round of EU enlargement," said Peter Stanovnik, head of the Institute of Economic Research at Ljubljana Economic Faculty.

"That would inflict a great deal of damage and slow down Slovenia's development. The country would miss out on the flow of international knowledge, technology, investment and financial help," he added.

Slovenia's economy is expected to grow four percent this year, up from 3.1 percent in 1996, but experts say the country must change its attitude to foreign investors if it wants to keep that expansion on track.

"Slovenia needs to overcome its fear of foreigners, of foreign capital and of investing abroad. It needs to open itself towards the world," said Igor Luksic, professor of politics at Ljubljana's Faculty of Social Sciences.
So far Slovenia has employed one of most restrictive foreign investment policies in the region in order to prevent foreign buy-outs and minimise pressure on the local currency, the tolar.

"If Slovenia does not open up its capital market it will remain in the Balkans because domestic capital will not be sufficient to overcome the gap with the West," said Toni Apollonio, an analyst at bank A banka.
Foreign direct investment in Slovenia only represents about one percent of GDP and analysts said this figure needs to double within four years to ensure economic health.

The government has introduced a new bill on foreign exchange transactions which will liberalise foreign direct investment and remove the need for government approval. It is expected to be adopted by parliament later this year.
But the bill will leave control over key foreign portfolio investment in the hands of the central bank, which is standing by restrictions it has imposed on international investment.
Despite all the problems, however, experts say there is no going back on Slovenia's 1990 referendum that delivered 88 percent backing for independence from Belgrade.

"The benefits exceed the costs. I am sure that today over 90 percent of Slovenians would vote for independence again," said Joze Mencinger, director of the Economic Institute at Ljubljana University's Law Faculty.
